scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

In summary, the role of protector and provider fosters a cautious, thorough, and selfless decision-making style focused on stability and security, while also potentially affecting emotional well-being and relational dynamics.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being unreasonable in this situation with my dad and his business idea. Let me start by understanding the scenario again. I'm 26, and my dad is 55. We're complete opposites in personality. He's introverted and quiet, very intelligent but not great at getting things done. I'm more impulsive and headstrong, and while I'm not as intelligent as him, I do get things done. I guess I'm more traditional masculine compared to my dad. A couple of years ago, my dad came up with this business idea that was simple yet genius. I was amazed by it but didn't think he could pull it off because he's not the type to execute ideas. So, I took the idea and ran with it. I got the IP rights and started the business. It's been a massive success, not making millions yet, but into the six figures with the potential to make millions in the next half-decade if things keep going well. When I did this, my dad was very upset but didn't say much. My mom was proud and thought I did the right thing. I confronted my dad yesterday, and he called me a "fucking asshole," saying he felt betrayed and nearly cried. I told him straight up, "You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action." My sister walked in and started defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected it and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable. Is AITA (Am I The Asshole) here? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider a few things. First, the ownership of the idea. Did I "steal" it from my dad, or was it more about taking initiative? Then, the emotional impact on my dad. How did he feel about me taking his idea and running with it? Also, the financial aspectâĢĶoffering him a share of profits, but he rejected it. Plus, the family dynamicsâĢĶmy mom and granddad support me, but my sister supports him. I think it's important to look at the concept of intellectual property here. If my dad came up with the idea, does he have any claim to it? But I took the initiative to develop it, secure IP rights, and build the business. So, is it stealing, or is it taking an idea and making it a reality? Also, considering our personalities, my dad is more of an ideas person, while I'm the executor. So, in a way, I'm using my strengths to bring his idea to life. But does that mean I should share the profits with him, or is it solely my venture? Emotionally, my dad felt betrayed. That's a strong reaction. Betrayal implies a violation of trust. Did I violate his trust by taking his idea without discussing it first? Or was it more about him feeling that I took something that was his? I also need to think about the offer I madeâĢĶ20% of profits. That's a significant offer, but he rejected it. Why? Maybe he feels that 20% isn't enough, or maybe he feels that the idea was his, and he should have a bigger share. Or perhaps he's hurt and doesn't want to accept anything from me. Family dynamics are also at play here. My mom and granddad support me, which is good, but my sister is on my dad's side. This could create tension within the family. How do I handle that? Another angle is the cultural or societal expectations. In many cultures, respecting and supporting family members, especially parents, is highly valued. Did I act in a way that aligns with those expectations, or did I prioritize my own ambitions over family harmony? Also, considering the long-term implications. If I continue to build this business successfully, how will that affect my relationship with my dad? Is it worth the potential long-term damage for the success of the business? I should also reflect on my own motivations. Was I genuinely trying to help my dad by taking his idea and making it successful, or was I more focused on my own success and recognition? Understanding my own intentions can shed light on whether my actions were self-serving or altruistic. Moreover, communication plays a crucial role here. Did I discuss the idea with my dad before taking it? It seems like I didn't, which might have contributed to his feeling of betrayal. If I had communicated my intentions, perhaps he would have felt more involved and less hurt. In terms of fairness, is it fair for me to take his idea and profit from it without giving him a share? Or is it fair because I took the initiative and effort to develop it? There's a balance between recognizing the originator of the idea and rewarding the executor. I also need to consider the potential for collaboration. Could we have worked together on this idea? Maybe if I had approached him and suggested a partnership, it could have been a win-win situation. Instead, I went ahead on my own, which might have made him feel excluded. Another point is the concept of ownership. In business, ownership is often determined by who contributes whatâĢĶwhether it's the idea, the capital, the labor, etc. If I took the idea but provided the capital and labor, does that mean I own it entirely? Or should the idea alone give him a share? Additionally, the emotional impact on my dad is significant. Feeling betrayed can have lasting effects on a relationship. I need to assess whether the success of the business justifies the emotional toll it's taking on my dad and our relationship. I also wonder about the long-term consequences for me. If I continue down this path, how will it affect my reputation within the family and my own sense of self-worth? Is the success of the business worth the potential loss of a close relationship with my dad? Furthermore, I should think about alternative solutions. Could I have approached this differently to preserve the relationship while still pursuing the business idea? Maybe by involving him more in the process or finding a way to acknowledge his contribution without necessarily giving him a financial share. In summary, I need to evaluate the ownership of the idea, the emotional impact on my dad, the fairness of the profit-sharing offer, the family dynamics, and the long-term implications of my actions. By carefully considering each of these aspects, I can determine whether I'm being unreasonable in this situation.
